lessons.title: The anatomy of a candlestick
glossary: A mark encoding four prices for one time period: open, high, low, close (OHLC).
The first traded price of the period.
The last traded price of the period; the most information-rich of the four.
The extreme prices reached during the period.
The rectangle spanning open to close; its length measures net directional conviction.
The thin lines to the high and low; they mark prices that were reached but rejected.
Open-High-Low-Close, the four numbers summarizing a period's trading.

blocks.label: Read this first
blocks.html: Educational only — not financial advice. Trading and day trading carry a high risk of loss; a large majority of active day traders lose money over time. Everything here describes tendencies and mathematics, never certainties. Never risk money you cannot afford to lose. We will repeat this because it matters more than any pattern in this course.

A price chart is a compressed record of a negotiation. Every candle is the market answering one question: at what price did buyers and sellers agree, and how far did they wander getting there? The candlestick chart, formalized by Japanese rice traders and popularized in the West by Steve Nison, packs four numbers into one glyph.
Each candle covers a fixed time slice (1 minute, 5 minutes, 1 day…). It encodes the open (first price), the close (last price), and the high and low reached in between — collectively OHLC.

blocks.title: One candle, four prices
blocks.caption: The thick part is the body (open-to-close). The thin lines are wicks (shadows) reaching to the high and low. Body length = |close − open|; here the body is 2.0 and the total range (high − low) is 3.2.

items.label: Body
items.html: The rectangle between open and close. A long body means one side clearly won; the ratio body/range (here 2.0/3.2 ≈ 0.63) is a rough conviction score.

items.label: Wicks / shadows
items.html: The thin lines above and below. They mark prices reached but rejected — the period travelled there but did not settle. Long wicks are footprints of a fight.

items.label: Colour
items.html: Green/hollow = close > open (buyers netted the period). Red/filled = close < open (sellers netted it). Colour tells you direction, not magnitude — read the body for that.

blocks.html: Think of a candle as the box score of one inning. The open and close are who was ahead at the start and end of the inning; the high and low are the biggest leads either side ever held. A tie game with wild swings (long wicks, tiny body) tells a very different story than a blowout (long body, no wicks).

blocks.label: The close is king
blocks.html: Of the four prices, the close carries the most information: it is where the market settled after all the day's information was digested, and it is the price most institutional benchmarks and end-of-day systems use. When analysts say 'the level held,' they almost always mean on a closing basis, not an intrabar wick.

blocks.q: On a green candlestick, which is necessarily true?
options: The close is below the open
The close is above the open
blocks.explain: Green means price finished higher than it started: close > open, so buyers netted the period. It says nothing about the size of the wicks or the volume.

blocks.q: A candle has open 50, high 55, low 49, close 50.2. Its body is small relative to its range. This best describes a…
options: Near-doji: lots of movement, almost no net change
blocks.explain: Body = |50.2 − 50| = 0.2 while range = 55 − 49 = 6. A tiny body on a wide range is indecision — the market travelled six points net two-tenths.

lessons.title: Chart types and why they disagree
glossary: A chart connecting only closing prices; hides intrabar range.
A Western bar showing the same four prices as a candle with ticks for open/close.
A smoothed candle type using averaged prices; better for trend, worse for exact levels.
A jump between one period's close and the next period's open, leaving no trading in between.

blocks.html: Candles are one of several encodings of the same OHLC data. Knowing what each hides is part of literacy.

blocks.title: Three ways to draw the same data

tabs.label: Line
tabs.html: Connects closes only. Cleanest for spotting the big trend, but it discards the high, low, and open — you lose all intrabar drama and every wick.

tabs.label: OHLC bar
tabs.html: A vertical bar for the range with a left tick (open) and right tick (close). Same information as a candle, less visually loud. Preferred by some quants who find candle bodies distracting.

tabs.label: Heikin-Ashi
tabs.html: Each 'candle' uses averaged prices (close = average of OHLC; open = average of prior HA open/close). This smooths noise and makes trends obvious, but the plotted prices are no longer real prices — never place a stop off a Heikin-Ashi wick.

blocks.label: Heikin-Ashi hides real prices
blocks.html: Because Heikin-Ashi averages prices, the values you see are synthetic. It is a trend visualizer, not a source of executable levels. Beginners who set stops from HA charts are stopping off numbers that never traded.

A gap is a discontinuity: the open of a period sits away from the prior close with no trades in between, usually from news released while the market (or that symbol) was thin. Gaps matter because unfilled orders pile up behind them, and 'gap fill' — price returning to the pre-gap level — is a heavily watched tendency.

blocks.title: An overnight gap up

annotations.label: gap up — opens far above prior close

blocks.caption: Between candle 2's close (20.2) and candle 3's open (21.6) no trading occurred. The shaded band is the gap; many traders watch whether price later 'fills' it.

blocks.q: Why can a line chart make a stock look calmer than it was?
options: It plots only closes, hiding the intrabar highs, lows, and wicks
blocks.explain: A line chart connects closing prices only. All the intrabar range — the spikes and rejections captured by wicks — is discarded, so violent sessions can look smooth.

lessons.title: Timeframes and multi-timeframe context
glossary: Reading a higher timeframe for context and a lower one for timing.
The property that price structure looks similar across timeframes.
Small, mostly random price movement that carries little information.

blocks.html: The same stock is a different animal on a 1-minute chart versus a daily. Price structure is roughly fractal — trends and ranges recur at every scale — but the meaning of a move depends entirely on which scale you are on. A $0.30 swing can be the whole story on the 1-minute and invisible on the daily.

blocks.label: Top-down is a discipline
blocks.html: Professionals read top-down: establish the higher-timeframe trend and levels first, then drop to a lower timeframe only to time an entry already justified by the bigger picture. This one habit prevents most 'reacting to noise' errors.

blocks.q: Why do disciplined traders check the daily before trading the 5-minute?
options: To fix the higher-timeframe trend and key levels as context before timing an entry
blocks.explain: Top-down analysis: the higher timeframe supplies trend and levels; the lower one only times an entry that the context already supports. It prevents overreacting to noise.

blocks.q: Price structure being roughly 'fractal' means…
options: Similar trend/range structure recurs across timeframes
Wicks disappear when you zoom in
blocks.explain: Fractal structure means the same building blocks — trends, ranges, support/resistance — appear at every scale, which is why the same reading skills transfer across timeframes.

questions.q: The body of a candlestick spans…
questions.explain: Body = open-to-close; wicks reach to the high and low.

questions.q: Which price carries the most information and is used by most end-of-day benchmarks?
questions.explain: The close reflects where the market settled after digesting the session's information; most benchmarks and 'level held' claims are closing-based.

questions.q: A candle with open 50, close 50.2, high 55, low 49 is best called…
questions.explain: Tiny body (0.2) on a wide range (6.0) is indecision — lots of travel, almost no net change.

questions.q: Heikin-Ashi candles are dangerous for stop placement because…
options: Their plotted prices are averaged and synthetic, not real traded prices
questions.explain: HA averages prices, so its wicks show numbers that never actually traded — a bad basis for a real stop.

questions.q: An unfilled 'gap' is…
options: A jump from one close to the next open with no trading between
questions.explain: A gap is a price discontinuity where no trades occurred; the untraded band is watched for a later 'fill'.

questions.q: Top-down multi-timeframe analysis means…
options: Establish trend/levels on a higher timeframe, then time entries on a lower one
questions.explain: Context from the higher timeframe, timing from the lower — the standard disciplined workflow.

questions.q: A line chart can understate volatility because it…
options: Plots only closes and discards intrabar highs/lows/wicks
questions.explain: Connecting closes hides all the intrabar range that candles show through their wicks.

modules.title: Trend Structure, Support & Resistance
modules.tagline: The skeleton of every chart: swings, structure breaks, levels, and the polarity flip.
objectives: Define trend objectively via swing structure (HH/HL, LH/LL) and identify BOS vs ChoCh.
Locate support and resistance as zones and explain the order-flow reason levels react.
Apply polarity: predict when broken resistance becomes support and distinguish a real break from a trap.
Draw trendlines and channels with discipline, avoiding overfitting.

lessons.title: Trend as market structure
glossary: The prevailing direction of price: up, down, or sideways.
A local peak/trough that anchors trend structure.
The swing sequence defining an uptrend.
The swing sequence defining a downtrend.
A close beyond the prior swing that confirms trend continuation.
The first swing that breaks the trend's pattern, hinting at reversal.

blocks.html: Price does three things: trend up, trend down, or range. Naming the current regime is the first decision a trader makes because the correct strategy inverts between them. We define trend not by a feeling but by the sequence of swing points.

An uptrend is a sequence of higher highs (HH) and higher lows (HL): each pullback bottoms above the last. A downtrend is the mirror — lower highs and lower lows. The trend is intact until a swing violates the pattern.

blocks.title: Uptrend: HH and HL, then a break of structure
blocks.caption: Each dip bottoms higher (rising green line = dynamic support). A close above the prior swing high (candle 6) is a break of structure confirming continuation.

blocks.html: The moment the pattern first breaks — an uptrend printing a lower low, say — is a change of character (ChoCh). It is not proof of reversal, but it is the earliest structural warning that control may be shifting.

cards.label: BOS (continuation)
cards.html: A close beyond the last swing in the trend's direction — uptrend takes out the prior high. Confirms the trend is still working.

cards.label: ChoCh (warning)
cards.html: A close beyond the last swing against the trend — uptrend prints a lower low. First hint the regime may be turning.

blocks.q: An established uptrend prints its first lower low. Structurally this is a…
options: Break of structure confirming the uptrend
Change of character warning of a possible reversal
blocks.explain: A lower low against an uptrend breaks the HH/HL pattern — a change of character. It warns of, but does not guarantee, a reversal.

blocks.q: The cleanest objective definition of a downtrend is…
options: A sequence of lower highs and lower lows
blocks.explain: Trend is defined by swing structure: lower highs and lower lows is a downtrend, independent of candle colour or indicators.

lessons.title: Support, resistance, and the flip
glossary: A price zone where buying has repeatedly halted declines.
A price zone where selling has repeatedly capped advances.
The tendency for broken resistance to become support and vice versa.
Sideways price oscillating between support and resistance.
Clustered stop and limit orders resting just beyond an obvious level.

blocks.html: Support is a price zone where buyers have repeatedly stepped in; resistance is where sellers have repeatedly capped a rise. They are zones, not lines — draw them with a highlighter, not a razor.

blocks.title: A range between support and resistance
blocks.caption: Price oscillates between a ~49.2 floor and ~50.9 ceiling. Range traders fade the edges (buy near support, sell near resistance) until a breakout ends the range.

blocks.label: Why levels 'work'
blocks.html: Levels are partly self-fulfilling: because many participants watch the same round numbers, prior highs, and session opens, resting orders cluster there. That clustering — a liquidity pool — makes a reaction more likely. It is order flow, not magic.

When a level breaks decisively, it often reverses roles: old resistance becomes new support and old support becomes new resistance. The mechanism is human: buyers who missed the breakout wait to buy the retest, and trapped sellers cover there. That confluence of orders defends the flipped level.

blocks.label: Levels break — plan for it
blocks.html: Support and resistance are tendencies, not walls. A break on rising volume flips polarity; a false break (poke without a close beyond) traps traders. Always pre-decide what a genuine break looks like (usually a close beyond the zone) versus a wick.

blocks.q: After resistance breaks decisively and price retests it from above and holds, that old resistance is now acting as…
blocks.explain: Polarity: broken resistance frequently flips to support because missed-breakout buyers and trapped sellers both create buying at the retest.

blocks.q: A 'false break' or bull trap is characterized by…
options: A decisive close beyond the level
Price poking beyond a level but closing back inside, trapping breakout traders
blocks.explain: A false break wicks beyond the level without a confirming close, then reverses — stranding those who chased the breakout.

lessons.title: Trendlines, channels, and drawing discipline
glossary: A sloped line connecting swing lows (up) or swing highs (down) acting as dynamic support/resistance.
A pair of parallel trendlines bracketing price.
Forcing a trendline through wicks to fit the past, reducing its predictive value.

blocks.html: A trendline is dynamic support or resistance: in an uptrend, connect successive higher lows; in a downtrend, connect lower highs. A second parallel line forms a channel that brackets the move.

blocks.title: An up-channel
blocks.caption: Two parallel lines bracket the advance. Traders buy pullbacks to the lower rail and trim near the upper rail while structure holds.

blocks.label: Don't overfit the line
blocks.html: Any three points can be connected if you cheat through wicks. A trendline earns trust by being touched and respected on a closing basis multiple times without being redrawn. If you find yourself moving the line to fit each new bar, it has no predictive value — you are overfitting the past.

blocks.title: Drawing a trustworthy trendline
steps: Start from two clear swing points in the trend direction (lows for up, highs for down).
Project the line forward; do not adjust it to chase price.
Count clean touches. Two points define a line; the third respected touch validates it.
Decide in advance: a decisive close through the line ends it. That is also a logical stop location.

blocks.q: What most reduces a trendline's usefulness?
options: Drawing it once and leaving it
Constantly redrawing it through wicks to fit new bars (overfitting)
blocks.explain: A line you keep moving to fit the past has no forward value. Trustworthy lines are anchored, extended, and left alone to be tested.

blocks.q: In an up-channel, a disciplined trader typically…
options: Buys the upper rail and sells the lower
Buys pullbacks toward the lower rail and trims near the upper rail while structure holds
Only trades the breakout of the daily
blocks.explain: In an up-channel you buy weakness (pullbacks to the rising lower rail = support) and take profits into strength (upper rail = resistance), until structure breaks.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Edwards & Magee, "Technical Analysis of Stock Trends"
The foundational classic on trendlines, channels, and classical chart patterns — primary source for level-drawing discipline.
Murphy, "Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets"
The standard comprehensive reference tying trend structure and support/resistance together.
Brooks, "Trading Price Action Trends"
Bar-by-bar treatment of trend structure, swings, and breaks for serious price-action study.

questions.q: An uptrend is defined structurally by…
questions.explain: Trend = swing structure. HH + HL is an uptrend regardless of colour or indicators.

questions.q: A 'change of character' (ChoCh) in an uptrend is…
options: The first lower low that breaks the HH/HL pattern
questions.explain: The first swing that violates the trend's structure warns of a possible regime change.

questions.q: Broken resistance that price retests from above and holds becomes…
questions.explain: Polarity: trapped sellers and missed-breakout buyers create support at the retest of old resistance.

questions.q: A bull trap / false break is…
options: A poke above a level that closes back inside, trapping breakout buyers
questions.explain: No confirming close beyond the level; price reverses back into the range.

questions.q: The order-flow reason levels react is that…
options: Resting orders cluster at widely watched levels (liquidity pools)
questions.explain: Clustered orders at watched levels make reactions more likely — partly self-fulfilling order flow.

questions.q: The best practice for a decisive break of a level is to require…
options: A close beyond the zone, ideally on rising volume
questions.explain: A closing break filters out wick-only false breaks; volume adds conviction.

questions.q: Overfitting a trendline means…
options: Anchoring it to two swings and leaving it
Repeatedly redrawing it through wicks to fit each new bar
questions.explain: A constantly redrawn line fits the past but predicts nothing.

modules.title: Candlestick Patterns & Price Action
modules.tagline: High-signal shapes, the psychology they encode, and the statistics that keep you honest.
objectives: Identify doji, hammer, shooting star, marubozu, engulfing, and inside bars and state the psychology each encodes.
Rank a pattern's reliability by location, trend fit, confirmation, and volume (confluence).
Treat any pattern as a conditional probability measured against its base rate.
Recognize confirmation, survivorship, and small-sample biases that manufacture false edges.

lessons.title: Single-candle signals and their psychology
glossary: A candle with open ≈ close (tiny body); indecision.
Small body up top, long lower wick; rejection of lower prices.
Small body at the bottom, long upper wick; rejection of higher prices.
A candle with little or no wick; one side dominated wire-to-wire.
A sharp move pushed back, leaving a long wick.

blocks.html: Some single candles hint that control is shifting. They are clues, not prophecies, and only carry weight in the right context: at a tested level, after an extended move, and confirmed by what follows.

items.label: Doji
items.html: Open ≈ close. Buyers and sellers fought to a draw. After a long trend, a stalemate warns momentum is tiring.

items.label: Hammer
items.html: Small body up top, long lower wick. Price fell then buyers reclaimed it by the close — rejection of lower prices. Meaningful at support.

items.label: Shooting star
items.html: Small body low, long upper wick. Buyers pushed up then sellers slammed it back — rejection of higher prices. Meaningful at resistance.

items.label: Marubozu
items.html: Almost no wick. One side controlled from open to close — maximal conviction for the period.

blocks.title: Hammer defending support
blocks.caption: Sellers drove price to ~9.9 but buyers reclaimed almost all of it by the close, printing a hammer right at support — a footprint of defense.

blocks.label: The wick tells the story
blocks.html: On a hammer, the long lower wick is the message: price was offered much lower and buyers absorbed it. The location (at support) and the follow-through (next candle) decide whether that absorption matters.

blocks.q: A shooting star at resistance suggests…
options: Sellers rejected higher prices — possible stall of the advance
blocks.explain: A long upper wick means price was pushed up then sold back down; at resistance that rejection warns the advance may stall. It is a clue, not a certainty.

blocks.q: A doji is most informative when it appears…
options: After an extended trend or at a tested level
blocks.explain: Indecision matters where a decision was expected — after a strong trend or at a key level — not in the middle of chop.

lessons.title: Multi-candle patterns and confirmation
glossary: A candle whose body fully covers the prior candle's body.
A candle whose whole range sits within the prior candle's range; compression.
Waiting for a following candle, close, or volume to validate a signal.

blocks.html: A bullish engulfing is two candles: a small red one, then a larger green one whose body fully covers it. It says sellers were decisively overpowered — strongest after a downtrend into support.

blocks.title: Bullish engulfing at a level
blocks.caption: The final green candle opens near the prior close and closes above the prior open — its body swallows the red body. Buyers overwhelmed sellers.

blocks.html: An inside bar is the opposite: a candle whose entire range sits inside the prior candle. It signals compression — a coiled spring — and traders often watch for the break of the mother bar's range.

head: Pattern
Reads as
Best context
rows: At support/resistance, with the higher-timeframe trend
In a trend as a continuation coil
After an extended move as an exhaustion warning
At a tested level, confirmed next candle

blocks.label: Context is everything
blocks.html: The identical candle shape means little in open space. Weight a pattern only when it appears at a tested level, aligns with the higher-timeframe trend, and comes with supportive volume. A pattern alone is a weak signal — Bulkowski's statistics show many patterns barely beat a coin flip in isolation.

blocks.title: How a trader actually uses a pattern
steps: Is it at a meaningful level? If not, ignore it.
Does it agree with the higher-timeframe direction?
Wait for the next candle / a confirming close / volume rather than front-running.
Define the invalidation (stop) and target before entering.

blocks.q: Why is a bullish engulfing at support more meaningful than one in open space?
options: Confluence — a tested level plus the pattern is a stronger, corroborated signal
blocks.explain: Confluence: the pattern lining up with a meaningful level and the trend makes it far more reliable than the shape alone.

blocks.q: An inside bar primarily signals…
options: Compression — reduced range that often precedes an expansion
blocks.explain: An inside bar's range sits within the prior bar: volatility is contracting, a coil that frequently precedes a directional break.

lessons.title: The base-rate problem: patterns need statistics
glossary: The unconditional frequency of an outcome, ignoring the signal.
Seeking evidence that fits a belief and ignoring the rest.
Judging a method only from the winners that survived, ignoring failures.
The number of observations; small samples mislead.

blocks.html: The dangerous thing about patterns is that our brains are pattern-completion machines: we see hammers everywhere after price rose and forget the hammers that failed. Rigor means treating a pattern as a conditional probability, not a promise.

Ask: after this pattern in this context, how often does price move my way within N bars, and by how much versus the base rate? If a hammer is followed by a bounce 55% of the time but price bounces 52% of the time anyway, the hammer's edge is nearly nothing.

blocks.label: Three biases that fake an edge
blocks.html: (1) Confirmation bias — remembering wins, forgetting losses. (2) Survivorship bias — studying only the charts where the pattern 'worked.' (3) Small samples — ten trades prove nothing; noise dominates until dozens of trades accumulate.

blocks.caption: One hammer-at-support pattern, twelve times: about half bounce, half fail.

blocks.q: A pattern is followed by a bounce 55% of the time, but the market bounces 53% of the time regardless. The pattern's edge is…
options: About 2 percentage points — tiny, and easily noise in a small sample
blocks.explain: Edge is the lift over the base rate: 55% − 53% = 2 points. That is small and could vanish once you account for costs and sampling error.

blocks.q: Studying only the charts where a pattern worked is…
blocks.explain: Cherry-picking the survivors (the winners) inflates a method's apparent reliability — survivorship bias.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: Bulkowski, "Encyclopedia of Candlestick Charts"
Publishes measured performance and break-even failure rates per pattern — the antidote to anecdote.
Nison, "Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques"
Authoritative on pattern definitions and the psychology behind them.
Aronson, "Evidence-Based Technical Analysis"
A rigorous, skeptical statistical treatment of whether TA signals have real edge.
Kahneman, "Thinking, Fast and Slow"
Why humans over-see patterns — base rates, small samples, and cognitive bias.

questions.q: A hammer's long lower wick shows that during the period…
options: Price fell but buyers reclaimed it by the close
Sellers closed it at the low
questions.explain: Long lower wick = rejection of lower prices; buyers absorbed the sell-off before the close.

questions.q: A shooting star at resistance suggests…
options: Rejection of higher prices — possible stall
questions.explain: A long upper wick at resistance means sellers slammed price back down — the advance may stall.

questions.q: A bullish engulfing candle is…
options: A larger green body that fully covers the prior red body
questions.explain: Buyers decisively overpower sellers; the green body engulfs the prior red body.

questions.q: An inside bar signals…
options: Compression that often precedes a directional expansion
questions.explain: Its range sits inside the prior bar — contracting volatility, a coil before a break.

questions.q: The single biggest factor making a pattern trustworthy is…
options: Context — location, trend fit, confirmation, and volume
questions.explain: Confluence matters far more than the raw shape.

questions.q: A pattern works 56% of the time; the base rate is 54%. Its edge is…
options: About 2 percentage points — small and possibly noise
questions.explain: Edge is lift over base rate: 56% − 54% = 2 points, easily within sampling noise.

questions.q: Judging a pattern only from charts where it worked is…
questions.explain: Ignoring the failures inflates apparent reliability — survivorship bias.

questions.q: Before acting on a reversal candle a disciplined trader first…
options: Waits for confirmation and defines stop and target
questions.explain: Confirmation plus a pre-planned invalidation and target is the disciplined process.

modules.title: Volume & Moving Averages
modules.tagline: Participation and trend tools — with the actual formulas, used sparingly.
objectives: Use volume and relative volume to judge conviction, and recognize climax/exhaustion.
Compute and contrast SMA, EMA (k = 2/(N+1)), and VWAP, and state what each measures.
Explain why moving averages lag and where crossovers whipsaw.
Assemble genuine multi-source confluence instead of redundant, correlated indicators.

lessons.title: Volume: the conviction gauge
glossary: Shares (or contracts) traded in a period; a measure of participation.
Current volume vs the average for that time of day; flags unusual activity.
An extreme volume spike often marking exhaustion at a move's end.
A breakout that fails and reverses, typically on weak volume.

blocks.html: Volume is how many shares changed hands, drawn as bars beneath price. It is the closest thing to a lie-detector for a move: price up on high volume shows real participation; price up on thin volume can be a fragile drift.

Raw volume is less useful than relative volume (RVOL) — today's volume divided by the typical volume for this time of day. RVOL of 3× means three times normal participation; that is what makes a breakout credible or a spike suspicious.

blocks.title: Breakout confirmed by a volume surge
blocks.caption: Price chops under resistance on ~40 units, then breaks out as volume triples. The surge signals broad agreement, not a thin push.

blocks.label: Volume confirms, it doesn't lead
blocks.html: Volume is context for the price move, read together with it. A breakout on rising volume is more trustworthy; a breakout on falling volume more often becomes a fakeout and snaps back. But beware climax volume — a huge spike after an extended run can mark exhaustion, not continuation.

blocks.q: A breakout above resistance on 3× relative volume is generally read as…
options: More trustworthy — broad participation behind the move
blocks.explain: High RVOL signals many participants agreeing, making the move more credible than a thin, low-volume push.

blocks.q: A massive volume spike after a long, extended rally can indicate…
blocks.explain: Climax volume after an extended move can mark the last rush of buyers — exhaustion — rather than fresh continuation. Context and follow-through decide.

lessons.title: Moving averages: SMA, EMA, and VWAP
glossary: Simple moving average: the unweighted mean of the last N closes.
Exponential moving average: a weighted mean that reacts faster to recent price.
Volume-weighted average price; an intraday fair-value line, reset daily.
A fast MA crossing above / below a slow MA.

blocks.html: A moving average summarizes recent price as a line. The simple moving average (SMA) is just the mean of the last N closes; it weights every period equally and therefore lags.
The exponential moving average (EMA) weights recent prices more, so it turns faster. It uses a smoothing constant k = 2/(N+1):

blocks.code:
k = 2 / (N + 1)
EMA_t = P_t * k + EMA_{t-1} * (1 - k)

# Example, N = 10 -> k = 2/11 = 0.1818
# Newest close gets ~18% weight; the rest decays exponentially.

blocks.title: Price riding above a rising average
blocks.caption: The blue line is a 3-period average. Price holding above a rising average is a quick read that buyers are in control; the average also acts as dynamic support.

blocks.html: When a fast MA crosses above a slow MA (e.g. 50 over 200) traders call it a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. These are lagging, popular, and prone to whipsaw in ranges — useful as trend filters, poor as precise timing.

VWAP weights each price by the volume traded there and resets each day. It answers 'what is the average dollar's entry price today?' — the benchmark institutions grade their fills against, which is exactly why it attracts orders.

blocks.code:
VWAP = sum(price_i * volume_i) / sum(volume_i)   # cumulative from the day's open
# 'price_i' is typically the bar's typical price (H+L+C)/3.

blocks.label: MAs lag — by construction
blocks.html: Every moving average is built from past prices, so it always trails. It summarizes trend; it does not predict. In a choppy range, MA crossovers generate a stream of false signals — the classic 'whipsaw.'

blocks.q: The EMA reacts faster than the SMA of the same length because it…
options: Weights recent prices more heavily via k = 2/(N+1)
blocks.explain: The EMA's exponential weighting gives the newest close more influence, so it turns toward price sooner than the equally weighted SMA.

blocks.q: VWAP is reset…
blocks.explain: VWAP accumulates from the day's open and resets each session — it is an intraday fair-value benchmark.

blocks.q: For a 20-period EMA, the smoothing constant k equals…
blocks.explain: k = 2/(N+1) = 2/21 ≈ 0.0952 — the weight applied to the newest close.

lessons.title: RSI: measuring momentum and its formula
glossary: A bounded indicator that swings within a fixed range to gauge momentum.
Relative Strength Index; momentum on a 0–100 scale over N periods (default 14).
RSI above 70 / below 30 — stretched, not an automatic reversal.
Price makes a new extreme but the oscillator does not — a momentum warning.

blocks.html: An oscillator is a bounded momentum gauge. The Relative Strength Index (RSI), from J. Welles Wilder (1978), compresses the ratio of average gains to average losses over N periods (default 14) onto a 0–100 scale.

blocks.code:
# 1. Over N periods, split each change into gains and losses.
# 2. Average them (Wilder's smoothing):
RS = AverageGain / AverageLoss
RSI = 100 - ( 100 / (1 + RS) )

# If AverageLoss = 0, RSI = 100.
# RS = 1 (equal gains/losses) -> RSI = 50.

blocks.html: Intuition: RSI = 50 means gains and losses balanced. Above 70 is conventionally overbought (recent gains dominate); below 30 is oversold. Crucially these are stretched, not sell/buy buttons — in a strong trend RSI can pin above 70 for a long time.

head: RSI reading
Interpretation
Trap to avoid
rows: Shorting a strong uptrend just because RSI is 'high'
Catching a falling knife in a strong downtrend

blocks.html: Divergence is often more useful than raw levels: price prints a higher high but RSI prints a lower high (bearish divergence), hinting the new price extreme lacks momentum. It is a warning of weakening thrust, not a timing trigger by itself.

blocks.q: RSI is calculated as 100 − 100/(1+RS), where RS is…
options: Average gain divided by average loss over N periods
blocks.explain: RS = AverageGain/AverageLoss over the lookback (default 14); plugging into the formula maps momentum onto 0–100.

blocks.q: Price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high. This is…
options: Bearish divergence — the new high lacks momentum
blocks.explain: Diverging slopes — price up, momentum down — warn that thrust is fading behind the new price extreme.

blocks.q: RSI above 70 in a strong uptrend most reliably means…
options: Momentum is stretched, but it can stay overbought for a long time
blocks.explain: Overbought is 'stretched,' not 'reverse now.' Strong trends routinely hold RSI above 70; blindly shorting it is a classic error.

lessons.title: MACD: trend-momentum from EMAs
glossary: EMA(12) minus EMA(26); measures momentum via the gap between two EMAs.
EMA(9) of the MACD line; a smoothed trigger.
MACD line minus signal line; visualizes momentum acceleration.
Where MACD = 0, i.e. the two EMAs are equal.

blocks.html: The MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence), from Gerald Appel, turns two EMAs into a momentum reading. It has three parts:

blocks.code:
MACD line   = EMA(12) - EMA(26)     # gap between fast and slow EMA
Signal line = EMA(9) of the MACD line
Histogram   = MACD line - Signal line

# MACD > 0  -> fast EMA above slow EMA (up-momentum)
# MACD crossing above Signal -> momentum turning up
# Histogram growing -> momentum accelerating

items.label: MACD line
items.html: EMA(12) − EMA(26). Positive means the fast average is above the slow one — upward momentum. It crosses zero when the two EMAs are equal.

items.label: Signal line
items.html: A 9-period EMA of the MACD line — a smoothed trigger. MACD crossing above it is a bullish signal; below, bearish.

items.label: Histogram
items.html: MACD − Signal, drawn as bars. Growing bars = momentum accelerating; shrinking bars = momentum fading even before a cross.

blocks.html: Two distinct signals live in MACD: the signal-line cross (MACD crosses its own signal) and the zero-line cross (MACD crosses 0, i.e. the EMAs flip order). Like all EMA-derived tools, MACD lags and whipsaws in ranges; its histogram is the most forward-looking piece because it turns before the crosses.

blocks.label: MACD is not bounded
blocks.html: Unlike RSI, MACD has no fixed 0–100 range — its scale depends on the instrument's price, so 'MACD is high' is meaningless across different stocks. Read it for crosses, zero-line, and histogram shape, not absolute value.

blocks.q: The MACD line itself is defined as…
blocks.explain: MACD line = EMA(12) − EMA(26): the gap between a fast and slow EMA, a momentum measure.

blocks.q: The MACD histogram equals…
blocks.explain: Histogram = MACD line − signal line; its bars grow as momentum accelerates and shrink as it fades, often before a cross.

blocks.q: Why is comparing one stock's MACD value to another's meaningless?
options: MACD is unbounded and scales with the instrument's price
blocks.explain: MACD is in price units and unbounded, so its magnitude depends on the instrument. Read crosses and histogram shape, not absolute level.

lessons.title: Using oscillators without fooling yourself
glossary: The tendency for stretched prices to snap back toward an average.
Trading in the direction of momentum rather than fading it.
Repeated false signals in a choppy, directionless market.
When an indicator's past values change as new data arrives, faking hindsight accuracy.

blocks.html: The deepest mistake with oscillators is using a mean-reversion tool (fade the extreme) inside a trend where you should be trend-following — or vice versa. RSI 'overbought' is a sell in a range and a buy-the-dip signal in a strong uptrend. The regime decides the meaning.

tabs.label: In a range
tabs.html: RSI > 70 near range resistance is a fade: sell the stretched move back toward the middle. Oscillators shine in choppy, mean-reverting conditions.

tabs.label: In a strong trend
tabs.html: RSI > 70 is just strength. Fading it fights the tape. Here you use pullbacks (RSI dipping to ~40 then turning) to join the trend, not to counter it.

blocks.label: Match the tool to the regime
blocks.html: First classify the regime (trend vs range) from structure and MAs. Then choose the oscillator interpretation that fits: fade extremes in ranges, buy dips in trends. Skipping the regime step is why beginners get chopped up.

blocks.label: Beware repainting and hindsight
blocks.html: Some indicators (and many social-media 'signals') repaint — their past values change as new bars arrive, so backtests look magically accurate. Always test on data the indicator could actually have known at the time (no look-ahead).

blocks.q: RSI hits 75. When is that a sell signal rather than 'just strength'?
options: In a range near resistance (mean-reversion regime), not in a strong uptrend
blocks.explain: Interpretation depends on regime: fade the extreme in a range; in a strong trend RSI 75 is strength, and fading it fights the trend.

blocks.q: An indicator that 'repaints' is dangerous because…
options: Its historical values change as new data arrives, faking hindsight accuracy
blocks.explain: Repainting means past signals were not actually available in real time, so any backtest of it is contaminated by look-ahead bias.

lessons.title: Bid, ask, spread, and the order book
glossary: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
Ask minus bid; the immediate cost of a round trip and a liquidity gauge.
The stack of resting limit orders at each price level.
National Best Bid and Offer — the best bid and ask across all US venues.

blocks.html: Beneath every candle is a live auction. At any instant there is a bid (highest price buyers will pay) and an ask (lowest price sellers will accept). The gap between them is the spread — the immediate, invisible cost of trading.
The full stack of resting orders at each price is the order book (or depth-of-market). It shows how many shares wait to buy below and sell above — the supply/demand ledger that price walks through.

blocks.label: The spread is a real cost
blocks.html: If you buy at the ask (10.02) and immediately sell at the bid (10.00), you lose the 2-cent spread before any price move. Over hundreds of trades, spreads and commissions are a headwind that a genuine edge must overcome — they are why high-frequency 'scalping' is brutally hard for retail.

blocks.q: The spread is…
options: Ask − bid, the immediate round-trip cost
blocks.explain: Spread = ask − bid. Cross it to trade immediately; it is a real cost paid before any price move.

blocks.q: The order book (depth-of-market) shows…
options: Resting limit orders (size) waiting at each price level
blocks.explain: The book displays resting supply and demand — how many shares wait to buy and sell at each level.

lessons.title: Liquidity, order types, and slippage
glossary: The ease of trading size without moving price much.
An order to execute immediately at the best available price; crosses the spread.
An order to trade only at a stated price or better; may not fill.
The difference between expected and actual fill price.
Taking liquidity (crossing the spread) vs posting it (resting a limit).

blocks.html: Liquidity is how easily you can trade size without moving price. A deep book with tight spreads (a large, popular stock) is liquid; a thin book with a wide spread (a small-cap at lunch) is not. Liquidity is not constant — it evaporates around news and near the open/close.

blocks.title: Two order types you must understand

cards.label: Market order
cards.html: 'Fill me now at whatever's available.' You take liquidity and cross the spread — guaranteed execution, uncertain price. In thin markets it can walk the book and fill badly.

cards.label: Limit order
cards.html: 'Fill me only at X or better.' You post liquidity — certain price, uncertain execution (it may never fill). Safer for price, but you can miss the move.

blocks.html: Slippage is the gap between the price you expected and the price you got. A market order for more shares than sit at the best ask walks the book — filling at progressively worse prices. In illiquid names, slippage can dwarf the spread and quietly destroy a strategy that looked profitable on paper.

blocks.title: Why a big market order slips in a thin book

annotations.label: market buy walks the thin ask stack

blocks.caption: With little resting size, a large market buy consumes each ask level in turn and fills far above the touch — that jump is slippage, not a 'move' you predicted.

blocks.label: Liquidity is when you need it least
blocks.html: Spreads widen and depth vanishes exactly when volatility spikes — news, halts, the first minutes of the session. That is when market orders slip worst and stops fill far from their trigger. Prefer limits in thin conditions, and size down.

blocks.q: You send a market buy larger than the size resting at the best ask. You will likely…
options: Walk the book and fill at progressively higher prices (slippage)
blocks.explain: A market order takes whatever liquidity exists; exceeding the top level walks up the ask stack, producing slippage above the quoted price.

blocks.q: A limit order trades price certainty for…
options: Execution uncertainty — it may never fill
blocks.explain: Limits fill only at your price or better, so you control price but risk not being filled at all.

blocks.q: Which best describes a 'taker'?
options: Sends a marketable order that crosses the spread and removes liquidity
blocks.explain: A taker crosses the spread with a marketable order, consuming resting liquidity; a maker posts a resting limit that adds it.

lessons.title: Who is on the other side: participants and games
glossary: A firm continuously quoting both bid and ask, earning the spread for providing liquidity.
A push to trigger clustered stops, generating fills before reversing.
The risk that whoever trades against you knows more than you do.
US pattern-day-trader rule: 4+ day trades/5 days needs $25k equity in a margin account.

blocks.html: Every fill has a counterparty. Some are market makers earning the spread for providing liquidity; some are institutions working large orders over hours; some are algorithms hunting the very stop clusters this course taught you to see. Understanding the game changes how you place orders.

A liquidity grab (colloquially 'stop hunt') is a sharp poke beyond an obvious level — just past yesterday's low, say — where retail stops cluster. Triggering those stops creates a burst of market sell orders that larger players buy into, then price reverses. This is exactly the false-break trap from Module 2, viewed from the order-flow side.

blocks.label: Adverse selection
blocks.html: When your limit order fills instantly, ask why someone was so eager to take the other side. Often it is because news you haven't seen is arriving — adverse selection. Being filled is not the same as being right; informed flow tends to pick off stale quotes.

blocks.label: Rules of the game (US)
blocks.html: The Pattern Day Trader rule requires ≥$25,000 equity in a margin account to place 4+ day trades within 5 business days. Leverage, margin calls, and locate requirements for shorting are structural constraints — know your venue's rules before, not after.

blocks.q: A sharp poke just below an obvious support (yesterday's low) that triggers stops then reverses is a…
blocks.explain: Larger players push through clustered stops to source liquidity, absorbing the triggered market orders before price reverses — the order-flow view of a false break.

blocks.q: Your resting limit fills instantly right before a sharp adverse move. This illustrates…
options: Adverse selection — the counterparty likely knew more
blocks.explain: Eager counterparties are often trading on information; being filled by informed flow is adverse selection, not a good sign.

modules.title: Risk Management & Position Sizing
modules.tagline: The actual edge: R-multiples, expectancy, drawdown math, and the Kelly ceiling.
objectives: Compute position size from a fixed-fractional rule and express outcomes in R-multiples.
Calculate expectancy = (W×avgWinR) − (L×avgLossR) and the breakeven win rate 1/(1+b).
Explain drawdown recovery asymmetry and why small fixed risk ensures survival.
Use the Kelly fraction f* = W − (1−W)/b as a ceiling, not a target.

lessons.title: R-multiples and position sizing
glossary: The dollar distance from entry to stop × shares — the amount risked on the trade.
A trade's result expressed in units of R (a +2R trade made twice the amount risked).
Risking a constant fraction (e.g. 1%) of equity per trade.
Planned reward divided by planned risk before entering.

blocks.html: You cannot control whether a trade wins. You can control how much you lose when it doesn't. That single asymmetry is why professionals obsess over risk, and it is best expressed in R-multiples.

R is your initial risk: the distance from entry to stop, times shares. Every outcome is then measured in R. Lose exactly to your stop = −1R. Make twice what you risked = +2R. Thinking in R makes trades comparable across different prices and account sizes.

blocks.code:
R (per share) = |entry - stop|
Shares       = (account * risk_fraction) / R_per_share
R ($)        = shares * R_per_share  = account * risk_fraction

# Example: $25,000 account, risk 1% = $250 per trade.
# Entry 20.00, stop 19.50  ->  R_per_share = 0.50
# Shares = 250 / 0.50 = 500 shares
# If it hits the stop: loss = 500 * 0.50 = $250 = 1R (the planned 1%).

blocks.label: Size is set by the stop, not by excitement
blocks.html: Notice what the formula does: a wider stop forces fewer shares, a tighter stop allows more, but the dollar risk stays fixed at 1% either way. You decide where you're wrong first, then arithmetic decides size. This is fixed-fractional sizing.

blocks.q: Your account is $20,000 and you risk 1% per trade. Entry 30.00, stop 29.60. How many shares?
A trade that makes three times what you risked is…
blocks.explain: Expressed in R-multiples, making three times the initial risk is a +3R result, regardless of the dollar amounts.

blocks.q: If you widen your stop but keep risk at 1% of equity, your share count…
blocks.explain: Wider stop = larger R/share = fewer shares to keep dollar risk fixed at 1%. Size and stop move inversely.

lessons.title: Expectancy: the equation of an edge
glossary: Average profit/loss per trade in R; the core measure of an edge.
Fraction of trades that are winners.
Average winning R divided by average losing R.
The win rate at which expectancy is zero for a given payoff.

blocks.html: A method's edge is captured by one number: expectancy — the average R you make per trade over many trades. It fuses win rate and payoff into a single verdict.

blocks.code:
Expectancy (in R) = (W * avgWinR) - (L * avgLossR)
  where L = 1 - W, and if losers = 1R then avgLossR = 1.

# Simplified when losers are exactly 1R:
Expectancy = (W * b) - (1 - W)          # b = avgWinR (payoff)

# Example: W = 0.40, average winner = +2R, average loser = -1R
Expectancy = (0.40 * 2) - (0.60 * 1) = 0.80 - 0.60 = +0.20R per trade

blocks.html: That +0.20R means: risking 1% per trade, you net about +0.20% of equity per trade on average, before costs. Over 200 trades that compounds meaningfully — but only on average, and only if you actually take the setup the same way every time.
For a given payoff b, the breakeven win rate — where expectancy = 0 — is W* = 1/(1+b). This is why a high win rate is not the goal:

head: Payoff b (avg win in R)
Breakeven win rate W* = 1/(1+b)
Meaning
rows: Must win over half just to break even
Can be wrong 2 of 3 times and still profit
Wrong 3 of 4 times and still profit
Small winners demand a very high win rate

blocks.label: Costs eat expectancy
blocks.html: The formula above ignores spread, commissions, and slippage. A gross +0.20R edge can become negative once you subtract, say, 0.05R of costs per trade × many trades. Always compute expectancy net of realistic costs — this is why overtrading a thin edge loses.

blocks.q: A system wins 40% of the time; winners average +2R, losers −1R. Its expectancy is…
With a 2:1 average payoff, the breakeven win rate is…
blocks.explain: W* = 1/(1+b) = 1/(1+2) = 1/3 ≈ 33.3%. Above that, the system is profitable.

blocks.q: Why can a 35% win rate still be highly profitable?
options: If the payoff ratio is large enough (e.g. 3:1), breakeven is only 25%
Win rate is all that matters
blocks.explain: Expectancy blends win rate and payoff. With 3:1 winners, breakeven is 25%, so 35% wins yields positive expectancy.

lessons.title: Drawdown, ruin, and the Kelly ceiling
glossary: A peak-to-trough decline in account equity.
The probability of losing enough capital to be unable to continue.
The bet size maximizing long-run growth; f* = W − (1−W)/b.
Random clustering of losses even in a positive-expectancy system.

blocks.html: Positive expectancy is necessary but not sufficient: path matters. Even a good system suffers losing streaks, and a drawdown that is too deep ends the game before the edge can compound. Survival is the first objective.

Losing streaks are longer than intuition suggests. With a 40% win rate, runs of 5–8 consecutive losers are ordinary over a few hundred trades. If each loss is 1% of equity, an 8-loss streak is roughly an 8% drawdown — survivable. At 5% risk per trade, that same streak is a devastating ~34% drawdown that needs a +52% gain to recover.

blocks.label: The recovery math is merciless
blocks.html: Losses and the gains needed to undo them are asymmetric: down 50% needs +100% just to break even. This asymmetry is the entire argument for small, fixed risk per trade — it keeps drawdowns in the shallow, recoverable zone.

The Kelly fraction gives the bet size maximizing long-run growth: f* = W − (1−W)/b. It is best used as a ceiling, not a target: full Kelly produces wild swings, and any error in estimating W or b (which are always uncertain) can push you past the growth-optimal point into decline. Most professionals trade a small fraction of Kelly — 'half-Kelly' or less.

blocks.code:
Kelly f* = W - (1 - W)/b

# W = 0.40, b = 2:  f* = 0.40 - 0.60/2 = 0.40 - 0.30 = 0.10 (10%)
# Full Kelly here says 'risk 10% per trade' -> enormous swings.
# Practitioners use a fraction (e.g. 1-2%), trading growth for smoother equity
# and a large safety margin against mis-estimated W and b.

blocks.q: Recovering from a 50% drawdown requires a gain of…
blocks.explain: From half your capital you must double it: +100% just to return to the prior peak. The asymmetry is why small risk matters.

blocks.q: Full-Kelly sizing is usually avoided because…
options: It produces large swings and any error in estimating W or b can push you past the optimum
blocks.explain: Full Kelly maximizes theoretical growth but is highly volatile and unforgiving of the inevitable estimation error in W and b; fractional Kelly is safer.

blocks.q: Why is small, fixed per-trade risk (e.g. 1%) the core survival tool?
options: It keeps ordinary losing streaks in the shallow, recoverable drawdown zone
blocks.explain: Small fixed risk means even a long losing streak produces only a modest, recoverable drawdown, keeping you in the game for the edge to compound.

modules.title: Psychology & Statistics of Trading
modules.tagline: Why edges live in samples and lose in emotions — variance, bias, and the journal.
objectives: Explain variance, sample size, and the law of large numbers, and why small samples mislead.
Identify loss aversion, the disposition effect, recency bias, gambler's fallacy, and revenge trading.
Use a written plan and journal to pre-commit decisions and separate process from outcome.
Compute realized expectancy from journalled trades to verify (or reject) an edge.

lessons.title: Probability, variance, and the law of large numbers
glossary: Averages converge to expectancy only over many trials.
Dispersion of outcomes around the mean; the source of streaks.
Number of trades; small samples are dominated by luck.
Confusing one lucky path with the true long-run expectation.

blocks.html: A trading edge is a statistical claim, and statistics only speaks over samples. Expectancy is the long-run average; any short run is dominated by variance. The law of large numbers promises convergence to your edge only after many trades — dozens at minimum, ideally hundreds.

Concretely: a +0.2R edge over 10 trades is invisible — a couple of unlucky losers swamp it. The same edge over 300 trades is a smooth uptrend in equity. Judging a method (or yourself) on a handful of trades is a category error.

blocks.caption: Many random paths, one +0.2R edge: early dips are variance, drift wins.

blocks.label: Small samples lie in both directions
blocks.html: A losing system can look brilliant for 15 trades; a winning system can look broken for 15. Never conclude from a small sample — and never let a hot streak convince you to abandon your rules or size up.

blocks.q: Why can a positive-expectancy system show a loss over 12 trades?
options: Variance dominates small samples; the edge only emerges over many trades
blocks.explain: Over few trades, random dispersion (variance) swamps a small average edge. The law of large numbers only guarantees convergence over many trials.

blocks.q: The minimum reasonable sample to start judging a discretionary edge is closer to…
blocks.explain: Meaningful conclusions need dozens to hundreds of trades so that variance averages out and expectancy shows through.

lessons.title: Cognitive biases at the trading desk
glossary: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good.
Selling winners too early and holding losers too long.
Over-weighting the most recent trades or events.
Believing a streak makes the opposite outcome 'due'.
Trading emotionally to recoup a loss, abandoning the plan.

blocks.html: The market is an engine for exploiting predictable human error. Kahneman and Tversky's work shows our decision-making is systematically biased — and every bias has a direct, expensive analog at the trading desk.

blocks.title: Five biases and their trading cost

items.label: Loss aversion
items.html: Losses feel ~2× as bad as equal gains. Result: we cut winners fast (to bank a good feeling) and let losers run (to avoid the pain of realizing them) — the exact opposite of 'let winners run, cut losers.'

items.label: Disposition effect
items.html: The direct consequence of loss aversion: selling winners too early, holding losers too long. It quietly inverts your payoff ratio.

items.label: Recency bias
items.html: Over-weighting the last few trades — sizing up after a hot streak, freezing after losses — instead of trusting the tested edge.

items.label: Gambler's fallacy
items.html: 'Five reds, so green is due.' Independent outcomes have no memory; a losing streak does not make a winner 'owed.'

items.label: Revenge trading
items.html: Trading to 'get back' at the market after a loss — oversized, unplanned, emotional. The single fastest route to ruin.

blocks.label: The plan is a bias-defeating device
blocks.html: A written plan — fixed entry, stop, size, and target decided before the trade — exists precisely to overrule the in-the-moment brain. You pre-commit while calm so the emotional you can't renegotiate. This is why journals and checklists work: they externalize discipline.

lessons.title: The trading journal as a scientific instrument
glossary: A structured log of every trade's plan, execution, and outcome for later analysis.
Judging decision quality separately from the (partly random) result.
Computing realized expectancy from journalled results to verify an edge.

blocks.html: Because outcomes are noisy, you cannot improve by staring at your P&L. You improve by treating trading as an experiment: log a falsifiable plan, execute it, and analyze the record. The journal is the instrument that turns gambling into science.

The key discipline is separating process from outcome. A trade can be well-executed and lose (good process, bad luck) or reckless and win (bad process, good luck). Rewarding yourself for lucky wins trains disaster. Grade the decision, then let statistics grade the results over many trades.

Makes the trade falsifiable and checks discipline
Feeds realized expectancy and slippage analysis
Separates process errors from bad luck

blocks.label: What the journal computes for you
blocks.html: With ~30+ logged trades you can compute realized win rate, average win R, average loss R, and expectancy — and compare planned vs actual to isolate slippage and discipline leaks. That is a feedback loop; raw P&L is not.

lessons.title: Specifying a rules-based setup
glossary: Entry/exit conditions specific enough that two people would trade them identically.
The precise event that initiates entry (e.g. a close beyond a level).

blocks.label: Capstone disclaimer
blocks.html: Educational only — not financial advice. Trading and day trading carry a high risk of loss; a large majority of active day traders lose money over time. Everything here describes tendencies and mathematics, never certainties. Never risk money you cannot afford to lose. This capstone builds a testing discipline, not a money-making system. The goal is the process of specification, backtesting, and honest evaluation — most simple retail setups have little or no edge after costs, and finding that out is a successful outcome.

A setup is only testable if it is mechanical: written so precisely that two people reading it would place the same trade. Vague rules ('buy when it looks strong') cannot be backtested and invite discretion creep. We will fully specify one classic setup: the support-flip breakout retest, synthesizing the whole course.

blocks.title: The five things every rule set must define
steps: Which instruments, which chart (e.g. liquid large-caps, 5-minute, regular hours only).
The exact event: e.g. price breaks resistance on RVOL ≥ 2, pulls back, and prints a bullish confirmation candle holding above the flipped level.
Exact location: e.g. a close back below the flipped level.
Exact rule: e.g. fixed 2R target, or trail under each new higher low.

blocks.q: Why must a setup be fully mechanical to backtest it?
options: So the rules are unambiguous and two people would trade them identically — otherwise results aren't reproducible
blocks.explain: Backtesting requires unambiguous rules; any discretion means the historical results can't be reproduced or trusted.

options: A close back below the flipped level
blocks.explain: The idea is that the flipped level holds as support; a close back below it proves the idea wrong — that is the logical stop.

lessons.title: Backtesting honestly and computing expectancy
glossary: Applying rules to historical data to estimate performance.
Using information not available at decision time, inflating results.
Tuning rules to past noise so they fail on new data.
Data withheld from tuning, used to honestly test the rules.

blocks.html: A backtest applies your mechanical rules to historical bars and records each trade's R-multiple. Done honestly it estimates expectancy; done carelessly it manufactures a fantasy. Three traps ruin most amateur backtests:

head: Trap
What goes wrong
Guard
rows: Using the day's close to 'decide' an entry that happened intraday
Only use information available at the bar you act on
Tuning parameters until the past looks perfect
Keep rules simple; test on out-of-sample data
Subtract realistic per-trade costs from every result

blocks.html: The output you care about is realized expectancy in R, computed exactly as in Module 7, plus the distribution: win rate, average win R, average loss R, largest drawdown, and number of trades. One number without the sample size and drawdown is meaningless.

blocks.code:
# Pseudocode for scoring a journal of trades (each stored as an R-multiple)
results_R = [+2.0, -1.0, -1.0, +2.0, -1.0, +2.0, -1.0, -1.0, +2.0, -1.0]

n        = len(results_R)
wins     = [r for r in results_R if r > 0]
losses   = [r for r in results_R if r <= 0]
win_rate = len(wins) / n
avg_win  = sum(wins)/len(wins)          # +2.0R
avg_loss = sum(losses)/len(losses)      # -1.0R

expectancy = sum(results_R) / n         # average R per trade
# = (4*2.0 + 6*-1.0)/10 = (8 - 6)/10 = +0.20R per trade (gross)

# Now subtract realistic costs, e.g. 0.05R/trade -> net +0.15R.
print(win_rate, avg_win, avg_loss, expectancy)

blocks.label: A negative result is a real result
blocks.html: If your honest, cost-inclusive backtest shows expectancy ≤ 0, the correct action is to not trade it — that is the system working. Discovering an edge doesn't exist before risking real money is exactly what this discipline is for. Do not 'fix' it by curve-fitting until the past looks good.

blocks.q: Using the day's closing price to justify an entry that occurred mid-session is…
blocks.explain: You used information (the close) not available when the entry decision was made — look-ahead bias, which inflates backtest results.

blocks.q: Ten trades produce R-multiples summing to +2.0R. The expectancy is…
blocks.explain: Expectancy = total R / number of trades = 2.0 / 10 = +0.20R per trade (before costs).

blocks.q: An honest backtest shows expectancy of −0.1R after costs. You should…
options: Not trade it — the negative result is the system working
blocks.explain: A negative net expectancy means no edge; declining to trade it is the correct, disciplined outcome. Curve-fitting to fix it is self-deception.

glossary: Simulated trading with no real capital, to test execution and rules.

blocks.html: Now you assemble everything: specify the rules, journal at least 10 trades (backtested on historical charts or paper-traded forward), and compute your expectancy honestly. This is the capstone deliverable.

blocks.label: Paper money, real discipline
blocks.html: Educational only — not financial advice. Trading and day trading carry a high risk of loss; a large majority of active day traders lose money over time. Everything here describes tendencies and mathematics, never certainties. Never risk money you cannot afford to lose. Do this on paper or in a simulator. The point is to practice specification, record-keeping, and honest evaluation — never to justify risking real capital on an unproven setup.

blocks.title: Do this
steps: Write the five rule components (universe/timeframe, entry trigger, stop, target, size) so precisely a stranger could execute them.
Collect 10+ trades that met your entry trigger, backtested or paper-traded — include the losers you'd rather forget.
For each: planned entry/stop/target/size, actual result in R, followed-plan Y/N, one-line note.
Win rate, avg win R, avg loss R, and expectancy = total R / trades. Subtract realistic costs.
State whether the net expectancy is positive, and — critically — whether 10 trades is enough to trust it (it usually isn't).

blocks.title: Assignment: Build & backtest a rules-based setup
blocks.brief: Specify one fully mechanical setup, journal at least 10 trades (backtested or paper-traded), and compute its net expectancy in R. Submit the rule set, the 10-row journal, and your evaluation. Everything is simulated — no real capital.
items: A strong result states the universe, timeframe, exact entry trigger, stop (invalidation), target, and fixed-fractional size precisely enough that a stranger would trade identically.
A strong result includes a 10+ row journal with, per trade: planned entry/stop/target/size, actual R-multiple, followed-plan (Y/N), and a one-line note — losers included, not cherry-picked.

A strong result computes win rate, average win R, average loss R, and expectancy = (total R)/(number of trades), then subtracts realistic costs (spread + commission + slippage) to report NET expectancy.

A strong result correctly interprets sample size: it acknowledges that ~10 trades is dominated by variance and cannot confirm an edge, and proposes a larger forward/out-of-sample test before any conclusion.
A strong result treats a zero-or-negative net expectancy as a valid, honest finding (do not trade it) rather than curve-fitting the rules until the past looks profitable.
A strong result reflects on process vs outcome: identifies any trades that followed the plan yet lost (good process) or broke the plan yet won (bad process).

blocks.q: Your capstone's 10-trade backtest shows +0.3R expectancy. The most rigorous conclusion is…
options: The system is proven profitable — trade it live
Promising, but 10 trades is too small to trust; forward-test on more data before any conclusion
Win rate is all that matters
blocks.explain: Ten trades are dominated by variance; a positive figure is encouraging but not confirmation. Rigor demands a larger out-of-sample/forward test before trusting the edge.
